ref: Contra Noetum ch. 9 (chapter numbers identical in ANF vol. 5 and Lagarde 1858; Migne PG 10 uses the same chapter numbers). Not Marcovich.
greek: 9. εἷς θεός, ὃν οὐκ ἄλλοθεν ἐπιγινώσκομεν, ἀδελφοί, ἢ ἐκ τῶν ἁγίων γραφῶν. ὃν γὰρ τρόπον ἐάν τις βουληθῇ τὴν σοφίαν τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου ἀσκεῖν, οὐκ ἄλλως δυνήσεταί τούτου τυχεῖν, ἐὰν μὴ δόγμασι φιλοσόφων ἐντύχῃ· τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τρόπον, ὅσοι θεοσέβειαν ἀσκεῖν βουλόμεθα, οὐκ ἄλλοθεν ἀσκήσομεν ἢ ἐκ τῶν λογίων τοῦ θεοῦ.

Transcribed by visual reading of the page image; the OCR text layer was only a guide. Accents and breathings may contain errors; apparatus at foot of page noted where relevant.
english: There is, brethren, one God, the knowledge of whom we gain from the Holy Scriptures, and from no other source. For just as a man, if he wishes to be skilled in the wisdom of this world, will find himself unable to get at it in any other way than by mastering the dogmas of philosophers, so all of us who wish to practise piety will be unable to learn its practice from any other quarter than the oracles of God. Whatever things, then, the Holy Scriptures declare, at these let us took; and whatsoever things they teach, these let us learn; and as the Father wills our belief to be, let us believe; and as He wills the Son to be glorified, let us glorify Him; and as He wills the Holy Spirit to be bestowed, let us receive Him. Not according to our own will, nor according to our own mind, nor yet as using violently those things which are given by God, but even as He has chosen to teach them by the Holy Scriptures, so let us discern them.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

what_it_says: Christians must know the one God only from Scripture; the Scriptures are the sole rule for believing the Father, glorifying the Son and receiving the Spirit.
limits: Chapter 9 says nothing about the Trinity in itself; it sets the method (Scripture alone) for the rest of the treatise. Who the 'Son' and 'Spirit' are is argued in ch.10-18.

english: God, subsisting alone, and having nothing contemporaneous with Himself, determined to create the world. And conceiving the world in mind, and willing and uttering the word, He made it; and straightway it appeared, formed as it had pleased Him. For us, then, it is sufficient simply to know that there was nothing contemporaneous with God. Beside Him there was nothing; but He, while existing alone, yet existed in plurality. For He was neither without reason, nor wisdom, nor power, nor counsel And all things were in Him, and He was the All.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

limits: 'Existed in plurality' (αὐτὸς δὲ μόνος ὢν πολὺς ἦν) is the phrase a modalist or a Noetian reading will press; Hippolytus gives no account here of the Word as a distinct person before creation (Kelly, Hanson). english: And as the Author, and fellow-Counsellor, and Framer of the things that are in formation, He begat the Word; and as He bears this Word in Himself, and that, too, as (yet) invisible to the world which is created, He makes Him visible; (and) uttering the voice first, and begetting Him as Light of Light, He set Him forth to the world as its Lord, (and) His own mind; and whereas He was visible formerly to Himself alone, and invisible to the world which is made, He makes Him visible in order that the world might see Him in His manifestation, and be capable of being saved.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

what_it_says: God begets the Word as author, counsellor and framer of creation, and first utters him as a 'first voice' and as light from light, setting him forth to the world as its Lord and his own mind.
limits: The verb 'begat' (ἐγέννα) is the Arian point of attack: read as creation, not eternal generation. 'Light from light' and 'first voice' are the Logos-prolation vocabulary that critics (Loofs, Harnack, Kelly) read as a Logos not yet a distinct person until the creative act. Hanson and Simonetti defend a generation before the creation. [Scholars named here are cited from memory; I did not open their works. UNVERIFIED.]

greek: καὶ οὕτως παρίστατο αὐτῷ ἕτερος. ἕτερον δὲ λέγων οὐ δύο θεοὺς λέγω, ἀλλ' ὡς φῶς ἐκ φωτὸς ἢ ὡς ὕδωρ ἐκ πηγῆς ἢ ὡς ἀκτῖνα ἀπὸ ἡλίου. δύναμις γὰρ μία ἡ ἐκ τοῦ παντός, τὸ δὲ πᾶν πατήρ, ἐξ οὗ δύναμις λόγος. οὗτος δὲ νοῦς, ὃς προβὰς ἐν κόσμῳ ἐδείκνυτο παῖς θεοῦ. 'πάντα τοίνυν δι' αὐτοῦ,' αὐτὸς δὲ 'μόνος ἐκ πατρός.'

english: And thus there appeared another beside Himself. But when I say another, I do not mean that there are two Gods, but that it is only as light of light, or as water from a fountain, or as a ray from the sun. For there is but one power, which is from the All; and the Father is the All, from whom cometh this Power, the Word. And this is the mind which came forth into the world, and was manifested as the Son of God. All things, then, are by Him, and He alone is of the Father.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

edition: Lagarde 1858 (Teubner) for Greek; ANF vol. 5 (Hippolytus, Cyprian, Caius, Novatian; archive.org ante-nicene-fathers-vol-5, scan from CCEL, 2000 upload)
what_it_says: Hippolytus says 'another' does not mean two gods but light from light, water from a fountain, a ray from the sun; the Word is the one power that comes from the All (the Father), and is the Son.
limits: The images (ray, fountain, light from light) are the standard Nicene-era analogies but also the ones Arians and modalists both read in their own way. 'Power' (δύναμις) and 'of the Father' (ἐκ πατρός) are the words the Unitarian uses for a Son who is only a power. 'Μόνος ἐκ πατρός' is quoted from John, and Hippolytus does not say here whether this is a generation.

english: Acting then in these (prophets), the Word spoke of Himself. For already He became His own herald, and showed that the Word would be manifested among men. And for this reason He cried thus: "I am made manifest to them that sought me not; I am found of them that asked not for me.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

what_it_says: The Word speaks through the prophets about himself, announcing that he will appear among men (Isa 65:1 quoted).
limits: Chapter 12 is a bridge passage; it is not an argument for the Trinity. 'The Word spoke of Himself' is the kind of sentence a critic reads as the Word being a speaking voice of the Father. The Isaiah quotation is cited as the Word's own words.

ref: Contra Noetum ch. 13 (chapter numbers identical in ANF vol. 5 and Lagarde 1858; Migne PG 10 uses the same chapter numbers). Not Marcovich.
greek: 13. καὶ Ἱερεμίας λέγει· 'τίς ἔστιν ἐν ὑποστήματι κυρίου καὶ εἶδεν τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ;' λόγος δὲ θεοῦ μόνος ὁρατός, ἀνθρώπου δὲ ἀκουστός· ὅπου ὁρᾶν τὸν λόγον λέγει, ἀνάγκην ἔχω πιστεύειν ὁρατὸν τοῦτον ἀπεσταλμένον. οὐκ ἄλλος ἦν ἀλλ' ἢ ὁ λόγος. ὅτι δὲ ἀπεστάλθη, μαρτυρεῖ Πέτρος πρὸς τὸν ἑκατόνταρχον Κορνήλιον λέγων 'ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ διὰ κηρύγματος Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ.' εἰ δὲ οὖν λόγος ἀποστέλλεται διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρός ἐστι Ἰησοῦς χριστός.
greek_edition: Lagarde, Hippolyti Romani quae feruntur omnia Graece (Leipzig, Teubner 1858), printed pp. 52; read from the page image of archive.org hippolytiromani00lagagoog (PDF page = printed page + 21). Transcribed by visual reading of the page image; the OCR text layer was only a guide. Accents and breathings may contain errors; apparatus at foot of page noted where relevant.
english: Now Jeremiah says, "Who hath stood in the counsel of the Lord, and hath perceived His Word?" But the Word of God alone is visible, while the word of man is audible. When he speaks of seeing the Word, I must believe that this visible (Word) has been sent. And there was none other (sent) but the Word. And that He was sent Peter testifies, when he says to the centurion Cornelius: "God sent His Word unto the children of Israel by the preaching of Jesus Christ. This is the God who is Lord of all." If, then, the Word is sent by Jesus Christ, the will of the Father is Jesus Christ.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

edition: Lagarde 1858 (Teubner) for Greek; ANF vol. 5 (Hippolytus, Cyprian, Caius, Novatian; archive.org ante-nicene-fathers-vol-5, scan from CCEL, 2000 upload)
what_it_says: The Word is the one visible to God alone, sent (ἀπεσταλμένον) by the Father; Peter says God sent the Word through Jesus Christ, so the Father's will is Jesus Christ.
limits: 'Sent' (ἀπεσταλμένον, ἀπέστειλεν) is the subordinationist term (Arian, Unitarian). Hippolytus' answer is that the sent one is the Word who is God, and that the Father's will is Jesus Christ. The Jeremiah and Acts 10:36 quotations are Hippolytus' scripture proofs, not an analysis of 'sent'. Critics: Kelly, Simonetti. [Scholars named here are cited from memory; I did not open their works. UNVERIFIED.]

greek: 14. ταῦτα μὲν οὖν, ἀδελφοί, σημαίνουσιν αἱ γραφαί, ταύτην τὴν οἰκονομίαν παραδίδωσιν ἡμῖν καὶ ὁ μακάριος Ἰωάννης ἐν εὐαγγελίῳ μαρτυρῶν καὶ τοῦτον τὸν λόγον θεὸν ὁμολογεῖ οὕτως λέγων· 'ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.' εἰ δὲ οὖν ὁ λόγος πρὸς τὸν θεὸν θεὸς ὢν, τί οὖν φήσειεν ἄν τις· Δύο λέγεις θεούς; δύο μὲν οὐκ ἐρῶ θεούς ἀλλ' ἢ ἕνα, πρόσωπα δὲ δύο, οἰκονομίᾳ δὲ τρίτην τὴν χάριν τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος. πατὴρ μὲν γὰρ εἷς, πρόσωπα δὲ δύο,
greek_edition: Lagarde, Hippolyti Romani quae feruntur omnia Graece (Leipzig, Teubner 1858), printed pp. 52; read from the page image of archive.org hippolytiromani00lagagoog (PDF page = printed page + 21). Transcribed by visual reading of the page image; the OCR text layer was only a guide. Accents and breathings may contain errors; apparatus at foot of page noted where relevant.
english: These things then, brethren, are declared by the Scriptures. And the blessed John, in the testimony of his Gospel, gives us an account of this economy (disposition) and acknowledges this Word as God, when he says, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." If, then, the Word was with God, and was also God, what follows? Would one say that he speaks of two Gods? I shall not indeed speak of two Gods, but of one; of two Persons however, and of a third economy (disposition), viz., the grace of the Holy Ghost. For the Father indeed is One, but there are two Persons, because there is also the Son; and then there is the third, the Holy Spirit.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

what_it_says: John 1:1 shows the Word is God with God; Hippolytus says he speaks of one God, two 'prosopa' and a third 'economy', namely the grace of the Holy Spirit; the Father is one.
limits: The phrase is the central Trinitarian text, but 'πρόσωπα' here is not the later Nicene hypostasis/person (Kelly, Hanson, Prestige); the Spirit is named 'grace' ('χάρις') and 'third economy', not yet a person of equal kind. The Greek 'οἰκονομίᾳ' is the apparatus-attested reading (Lagarde p.52 l.29, see his note: Turrianus has 'οἰκονομίας'). [Scholars named here are cited from memory; I did not open their works. UNVERIFIED.]

greek: ὅτι καὶ ὁ υἱός, τὸ δὲ τρίτον τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα. πατὴρ ἐντέλλεται, λόγος ἀποτελεῖ, υἱὸς δὲ δείκνυται, δι' οὗ πατὴρ πιστεύεται. οἰκονομίᾳ συμφωνία συνάγεται εἰς ἕνα θεόν. εἷς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θεός. ὁ γὰρ κελεύων πατήρ, ὁ δὲ ὑπακούων υἱός, τὸ δὲ συνετίζον ἅγιον πνεῦμα. ὁ ὢν πατὴρ ἐπὶ πάντων, ὁ δὲ υἱὸς διὰ πάντων, τὸ δὲ ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἐν πᾶσιν.

Transcribed by visual reading of the page image; the OCR text layer was only a guide. Accents and breathings may contain errors; apparatus at foot of page noted where relevant.
english: and then there is the third, the Holy Spirit. The Father decrees, the Word executes, and the Son is manifested, through whom the Father is believed on. The economy of harmony is led back to one God; for God is One. It is the Father who commands, and the Son who obeys, and the Holy Spirit who gives understanding: the Father who is above all, and the Son who is through all, and the Holy Spirit who is in all.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

edition: Lagarde 1858 (Teubner) for Greek; ANF vol. 5 (Hippolytus, Cyprian, Caius, Novatian; archive.org ante-nicene-fathers-vol-5, scan from CCEL, 2000 upload)
what_it_says: The Father commands, the Logos executes, the Son is shown, through whom the Father is believed; the economy of harmony leads to one God. The Father commands, the Son obeys, the Spirit gives understanding; the Father is over all, the Son through all, the Spirit in all.
limits: This is the passage Arians and Unitarians cite: 'the Father commands, the Son obeys' (ὁ κελεύων ... ὁ ὑπακούων). Hippolytus gives 'economy' (οἰκονομίᾳ) as the reason for the difference and a single God as the result; the Spirit's role is 'understanding' and 'in all'. Defenders (Bull, Newman) read it as economic order; critics (Harnack, Prestige) read it as subordination. [Scholars named here are cited from memory; I did not open their works. UNVERIFIED.]

greek: Ἰουδαῖοι μὲν γὰρ ἐδόξασαν πατέρα, ἀλλ' οὐκ ηὐχαρίστησαν υἱόν γὰρ οὐκ ἐπέγνωσαν. μαθηταὶ ἐπέγνωσαν υἱόν, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, δι' ὃ καὶ ἠρνήσαντο. γινώσκων οὖν ὁ πατρῷος λόγος τὴν οἰκονομίαν καὶ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρὸς ὅτι οὐκ ἄλλως βούλεται δοξάζεσθαι ὁ πατὴρ ἢ οὕτως, ἀναστὰς παρέδωκεν τοῖς μαθηταῖς λέγων 'πορευθέντες μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, βαπτίζοντες αὐτοὺς εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος,' δεικνύων ὅτι πᾶς ὃς ἂν ἐν τι τούτων ἐκλίπῃ, τελείως θεὸν οὐκ ἐδόξασεν. διὰ γὰρ τῆς τριάδος ταύτης πατὴρ δοξάζεται. πατὴρ γὰρ ἠθέλησεν, υἱὸς ἐποίησεν, πνεῦμα ἐφανέρωσεν.

english: For the Jews glorified (or gloried in) the Father, but gave Him not thanks, for they did not recognise the Son. The disciples recognised the Son, but not in the Holy Ghost; wherefore they also denied Him. The Father's Word, therefore, knowing the economy (disposition) and the will of the Father, to wit, that the Father seeks to be worshipped in none other way than this, gave this charge to the disciples after He rose from the dead: "Go ye and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." And by this He showed, that whosoever omitted any one of these, failed in glorifying God perfectly. For it is through this Trinity that the Father is glorified. For the Father willed, the Son did, the Spirit manifested.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

what_it_says: The Word, knowing the economy, commands the disciples to baptise in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit (Matt 28:19); through this Trinity (τριάδος) the Father is glorified; the Father willed, the Son did, the Spirit manifested.
limits: Matt 28:19 is quoted as a Trinitarian formula; 'Trinity' (τριάδος) is used by Hippolytus for an economic triad, not yet the Nicene consubstantial Trinity. Text-critical and form-critical doubts about Matt 28:19 are raised by some scholars; the 'Trinity' word here is not proof of Nicene doctrine. Text checked against Lagarde only; the Matt 28:19 wording is as printed.

english: But some one will say to me, You adduce a thing strange to me, when you call the Son the Word. For John indeed speaks of the Word, but it is by a figure of speech. Nay, it is by no figure of speech. For while thus presenting this Word that was from the beginning, and has now been sent forth, he said below in the Apocalypse,

what_it_says: Objector: 'you bring me a strange word when you call the Son the Word'; Hippolytus replies that John calls the Word the Son's name, and that the Word who was from the beginning was sent; Rev 19:11-13 is the proof text.
limits: The argument proves only that the Word and the Son are the same person (Hippolytus' 'one Son'); it does not show the Word has equal divinity. The Rev 19 proof text is taken in Hippolytus' allegorical sense.

english: What Son of His own, then, did God send through the flesh but the Word, whom He addressed as Son because He was to become such (or be begotten) in the future? And He takes the common name for tender affection among men in being called the Son. For neither was the Word, prior to incarnation and when by Himself, yet perfect Son, although He was perfect Word, only-begotten. Nor could the flesh subsist by itself apart from the Word, because it has its subsistence in the Word. Thus, then, one perfect Son of God was manifested.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

edition: Lagarde 1858 (Teubner) for Greek; ANF vol. 5 (Hippolytus, Cyprian, Caius, Novatian; archive.org ante-nicene-fathers-vol-5, scan from CCEL, 2000 upload)
what_it_says: The Word is called Son because he was to become Son (προσηγόρευσε διὰ τὸ μέλλειν αὐτὸν γενέσθαι); the Word apart from flesh was not yet 'perfect Son' though perfect Word, only-begotten; one perfect Son was manifested.
limits: This is the sharpest hard passage in Contra Noetum. 'The Word, apart from flesh, was not yet perfect Son' and 'was to become Son' make the Son's sonship economic/incarnational, which Nicene orthodoxy rejects for the eternal Son (Kelly, Simonetti, Hanson, Bull's defence). Hippolytus keeps 'only-begotten' and 'perfect Word' for the Logos before the flesh; the defence (Bull, Newman) is that sonship here refers to the manifest sonship. The text does not say the Son was created. Verified as printed in ANF (Salmond) and read in Lagarde; Migne PG 10 OCR also has 'προσηγόρευς διὰ τὸ μέλλειν αὐτὸν γενέσθαι' (djvu line 78590). [Scholars named here are cited from memory; I did not open their works. UNVERIFIED.]

english: See then, brethren, how the vesture sprinkled with blood denoted in symbol the flesh, through which the impassible Word of God came under suffering, as also the prophets testify to me. For thus speaks the blessed Micah: "The house of Jacob provoked the Spirit of the Lord to anger. These are their pursuits. Are not His words good with them, and do they walk rightly? And they have risen up in enmity against His countenance of peace, and they have stripped off His glory." That means His suffering in the flesh.

limits: 'The impassible Word of God came under suffering' is the explanation of the suffering of the Son as the Word's suffering 'in the flesh'. Critics (Hanson, Prestige) see it as an attempt to separate the impassible Logos from the passible flesh; Patripassian and Noetian readings are the ones Hippolytus is refuting. english: But you will say to me, How is He begotten? In your own case you can give no explanation of the way in which you were begotten, although you see every day the cause according to man; neither can you tell with accuracy the economy in His case. For you have it not in your power to acquaint yourself with the practised and indescribable art (method) of the Maker, but only to see, and understand, and believe that man is God's work. Moreover, you are asking an account of the generation of the Word, whom God the Father in His good pleasure begat as He willed.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

what_it_says: Refusing to explain the Word's generation: no one can give an account of his own begetting or of the maker's art, and God the Father begat the Word as he willed.
limits: 'Begat as He willed' (ἐγέννησεν ὡς ἠθέλησεν) is the wording Arians exploit (generation by will, hence creature). Hippolytus rejects the question rather than answering it; Kelly and Hanson read this as an apophatic refusal, not an Arian premise. Text-critical: the line-end 'ἐξεῖπεῖν' is as printed in Lagarde. what_it_says: Be satisfied with John 3:6 ('what is born of the Spirit is spirit'); the prophet signals that the Word is begotten but the how is kept by the Father until the time he appoints. Ps 110:3 (LXX) 'from the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten Thee' is quoted.
limits: The quotation of Ps 110:3 LXX is the eternal-generation proof that later Nicene writers use; here it signals that the begetting is true but its manner is not revealed (Kelly). Critics (Harnack, Loofs) read the 'before the morning star' as a pre-temporal begetting that is not yet eternal. Lagarde's Greek 'ἐκ γαστρὸς' is printed as read. greek: 17. αὐτάρκεις αὗται αἱ μαρτυρίαι πιστοῖς ἀληθείαν ἀσκοῦσιν. οἱ δὲ ἄπιστοι οὐδὲν πιστεύουσιν· καὶ γὰρ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐκ προσώπου τῶν ἀποστόλων διεμαρτύρατο λέγον 'καὶ τίς ἐπίστευσεν τῇ ἀκοῇ ἡμῶν;' ὥστε μὴ γενώμεθα ἄπιστοι, μήποτε ἐφ' ἡμῖν τελεσθῇ τὸ εἰρημένον. πιστεύσωμεν οὖν, μακάριοι ἀδελφοί, κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν ἀποστόλων, ὅτι θεὸς λόγος ἐξ οὐρανῶν καταῆλθεν εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν παρθένον Μαρίαν, ἵνα σαρκωθεὶς ἐξ αὐτῆς, λαβὼν δὲ καὶ ψυχὴν ἀνθρωπίνην (λογικὴν δὲ λέγω), γεγονὼς πάντα ὅσα ἐστὶν ἀνθρώπου ἐκτὸς ἁμαρτίας, σώσῃ τὸν πεπτωκότα καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν ἀνθρώποις παράσχῃ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ.

english: These testimonies are sufficient for the believing who study truth, and the unbelieving credit no testimony. For the Holy Spirit, indeed, in the person of the apostles, has testified to this, saying, "And who has believed our report?" Therefore let us not prove ourselves unbelieving, lest the word spoken be fulfilled in us. Let us believe then, dear brethren, according to the tradition of the apostles, that God the Word came down from heaven, (and entered) into the holy Virgin Mary, in order that, taking the flesh from her, and assuming also a human, by which I mean a rational soul, and becoming thus all that man is with the exception of sin, He might save fallen man, and confer immortality on men who believe on His name.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

what_it_says: The creed-like statement: according to the apostles' tradition, God the Word came down from heaven into the holy Virgin Mary, took flesh and a rational soul, became all that man is except sin, to save the fallen and give immortality to believers.
limits: Anarthrous 'θεὸς λόγος' in the creedal sentence is the nearest Hippolytus comes to 'the Word was God' applied to the incarnate life; it is not a homoousios formula. Critics note that the 'rational soul' (λογικὴν) and the Word's 'coming down' are read by Arians as a heavenly being descending.

english: Thus then, too, though demonstrated as God, He does not refuse the conditions proper to Him as man, since He hungers and toils and thirsts in weariness, and flees in fear, and prays in trouble. And He who as God has a sleepless nature, slumbers on a pillow. And He who for this end came into the world, begs off from the cup of suffering.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.

what_it_says: Being God, he does not refuse human conditions: he hungers, toils, thirsts, flees in fear, prays in sorrow and sleeps on a pillow; he who as God has a sleepless nature begs off from the cup of suffering.
limits: This is the passage Muslim polemicists and Unitarians cite against a divine Christ (hunger, fear, sleep, prayer). Hippolytus' answer: the human attributes are the flesh's; the 'sleepless nature' is God's. Patripassian risk is not resolved in the text itself. 'ἄυπνον' (accent/breathing) is read from the image; check against the scan.

limits: Hippolytus explains the 'I lay it down of myself' as the power of Life, not the Father's power. Unitarians read the words as a human mortal's act; the text gives no account of the Father's or Spirit's part beyond the sentence about the Father in ch.18 end.

greek: ᾧ πάντα ὑπέταξεν πατήρ. αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος ἅμα πατρὶ καὶ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι ἐν τῇ ἁγίᾳ ἐκκλησίᾳ καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ἀμήν.
greek_edition: Lagarde, Hippolyti Romani quae feruntur omnia Graece (Leipzig, Teubner 1858), printed pp. 57; read from the page image of archive.org hippolytiromani00lagagoog (PDF page = printed page + 21). Transcribed by visual reading of the page image; the OCR text layer was only a guide. Accents and breathings may contain errors; apparatus at foot of page noted where relevant.
english: to whom also the Father hath put all things in subjection. To Him be the glory and the power, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, in the holy Church both now and ever, and even for evermore. Amen.
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (ANF vol. 5, section heading 'The Extant Works and Fragments of Hippolytus [Translated by the Rev. S. D. F. Salmond]'). Note: the earlychristianwritings.com page for the same text is labelled 'Roberts-Donaldson translation'; the attribution conflict is not resolved.
page: Lagarde p. 57 (Greek); ANF vol. 5 printed p. 561 (English, PDF page 597 of the scan)
edition: Lagarde 1858 (Teubner) for Greek; ANF vol. 5 (Hippolytus, Cyprian, Caius, Novatian; archive.org ante-nicene-fathers-vol-5, scan from CCEL, 2000 upload)
what_it_says: The closing doxology of the treatise gives glory and power to the Son together with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the holy Church, now and for ever.
limits: Lagarde's text ends the treatise at ch.18 with this doxology; there is no separate 'Conclusion' or 'Refutation' fragment in Lagarde or in the ANF section. A doxology joining Son and Spirit with the Father is not a homoousios statement, and Arians could read 'together with' as a formula of association.
